subChunks.title: Enums: Beyond Simple Constants
subChunks.hookHtml: You've seen enums used as simple named constants — but in Java, enums are full-blown classes. They can carry state, define methods, and even behave differently per constant. It's time to unlock their true power.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Basic Enums

An enum defines a fixed set of named constants. Each constant is a singleton instance of the enum type.

enum Direction { NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST }

You can use them in switch statements, compare with ==, and iterate with values().

Enums with State (Constructor + Fields)

Enums can have fields and constructors. Each constant passes arguments to the constructor.

enum Spell {
    FIREBALL(80), FROST(60), THUNDER(90), HEAL(0);

    private final int damage;

    Spell(int damage) {
        this.damage = damage;
    }

    public int getDamage() {
        return damage;
    }
}

Note: enum constructors are implicitly private. You cannot call new Spell(...) from outside.

Enum Methods and Built-ins

Every enum automatically gets these methods:

  • values() — returns all constants as an array
  • valueOf(String) — returns the constant matching the name
  • ordinal() — zero-based index of the constant
  • name() — the constant's name as a String
for (Spell s : Spell.values()) {
    System.out.println(s.name() + " deals " + s.getDamage());
}

Spell s = Spell.valueOf("FROST"); // returns FROST
System.out.println(s.ordinal()); // prints 1

Enums in Switch Expressions

Switch expressions (Java 14+) work beautifully with enums. The compiler enforces exhaustiveness when all constants are covered.

Spell chosen = Spell.THUNDER;
String school = switch (chosen) {
    case FIREBALL -> "Fire";
    case FROST    -> "Ice";
    case THUNDER  -> "Storm";
    case HEAL     -> "Holy";
};
System.out.println(school); // Storm

storyBeats.text: The Hall of Elemental Catalogues stretched endlessly — row upon row of glowing spell crystals, each labelled with its school and potency. Eldrin gestured at the display.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Apprentice, a novice treats enum constants as mere labels. A practitioner gives them memory — fields that record the truth of each spell.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Now iterate the registry with values() and you'll see every spell's true cost.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when routing by school, trust the switch expression. It will force you to handle every possibility — no constants left in the dark.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Inside public class Main, define a static enum Spell with four constants: FIREBALL(80), FROST(60), THUNDER(90), HEAL(0). Each constant stores its damage value via a private field and a constructor. Add a getDamage() method.

In main:

  1. Loop over Spell.values() and print each as NAME: damage (e.g. THUNDER: 90).
  2. Use a switch-expression on Spell.THUNDER to determine its school: FIREBALL→Fire, FROST→Ice, THUNDER→Storm, HEAL→Holy. Print the school.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Prints the school Storm for THUNDER

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why Java enums are more powerful than simple integer constants, and describe a scenario where adding fields and methods to an enum is clearly the right design choice — rather than using a separate class.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, create an enum Potion with three constants: HEALTH(50), MANA(40), ELIXIR(100). Each stores its restore value. Loop all potions and print NAME: value. Then use a switch-expression on Potion.ELIXIR to print its rarity: HEALTH→Common, MANA→Common, ELIXIR→Legendary.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A high-performance Set implementation designed exclusively for enum types, backed by a bit vector.
A Map implementation optimised for enum keys, using an array internally for O(1) operations.
The zero-based position of an enum constant as declared in the source. Avoid persisting ordinals — insertions can shift them.
An enum can declare an abstract method that each constant overrides individually, giving per-constant behaviour.
When switching on an enum, the compiler can verify all constants are handled, eliminating the need for a default branch.
Each enum constant is a single JVM instance. This makes enums a thread-safe Singleton implementation by design.
Spell.valueOf("FROST") returns the constant; s.name() returns the constant's name as a String. They are inverses of each other.

questions.questionHtml: Which built-in enum method returns an array of all constants in declaration order?
questions.explanationHtml: values() is a compiler-generated static method that returns all enum constants as an array in the order they were declared. valueOf(String) looks up a single constant by name, while ordinal() and name() are instance methods.
SILVER is the second constant (zero-based index 1), so ordinal() returns 1. name() returns the constant's identifier exactly as declared: GOLD.

questions.questionHtml: This enum code fails to compile. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.correctAnswer: Enum constructors cannot be public. Remove the public modifier from the constructor — it must be private (or package-private).
questions.explanationHtml: Enum constructors are implicitly private. Marking one public is a compile error because the Java specification forbids it — the language must prevent external instantiation of enum types. Remove public from the constructor declaration.

questions.questionHtml: When is it better to use an enum with fields rather than a plain class with public static final constants?
options: When the set of values is open-ended and may grow at runtime
When you need a fixed, closed set of named instances each carrying related data
When you need inheritance from another class
When you need to create many instances with varying state
questions.correctAnswer: When you need a fixed, closed set of named instances each carrying related data
questions.explanationHtml: Enums are ideal when the full set of valid values is known at compile time and each value may carry associated state. They provide type-safety, exhaustive switch checking, and built-in iteration. If the set is open-ended, or you need inheritance, a regular class is more appropriate.

subChunks.title: Records: Immutable Data Carriers
subChunks.hookHtml: How many times have you written a class with fields, a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString — all for a simple data container? Java 16 introduced records to end that boilerplate forever.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Is a Record?

A record is a special kind of class designed to be a transparent, immutable data carrier. You declare the components and Java generates everything else.

record Point(int x, int y) {}

This single line gives you: a canonical constructor, accessor methods x() and y(), equals(), hashCode(), and toString().

Auto-generated Members

Given record Spell(String name, int power), the compiler generates:

// Constructor
new Spell("Fireball", 80)

// Accessors (NOT getName — just name())
spell.name()   // "Fireball"
spell.power()  // 80

// Meaningful toString
spell.toString() // Spell[name=Fireball, power=80]

// Structural equality
new Spell("A", 1).equals(new Spell("A", 1)) // true

Compact Constructors for Validation

A compact constructor lets you validate or normalise inputs without repeating the parameter list. The assignment to fields happens automatically after the body runs.

record Spell(String name, int power) {
    Spell {
        if (power < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Power cannot be negative");
        name = name.trim(); // you can reassign components here
    }
}

Records Implementing Interfaces

Records can implement interfaces, making them useful as typed data objects in functional pipelines.

interface Describable { String describe(); }

record Spell(String name, int power) implements Describable {
    public String describe() {
        return name + " (power: " + power + ")";
    }
}

When Records vs Classes

  • Use a record when the type is purely a data carrier, immutability is desired, and equality is structural.
  • Use a class when you need mutable state, inheritance, or complex lifecycle management.

storyBeats.text: The Scriptorium was buried in boilerplate scrolls — every spell tome required pages of constructor incantations, getter sigils, and equality runes before a single useful word appeared.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Enough! The Academy adopted records precisely to banish this tedium. Declare what a spell is — its name and power — and the language provides the rest.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Equality is structural — two spells with the same name and power are equal. No manual equals() needed. And compact constructors let you enforce the laws of magic: no negative power.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Records can even implement interfaces. Make them Describable, Comparable — whatever the domain demands. They are fully first-class citizens, just immutable.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Define two records at the top of your file (outside Main or as static members):

  • record Spell(String name, int power)
  • record Wizard(String name, Spell signature)

In main:

  1. Create Wizard wizard = new Wizard("Eldrin", new Spell("Arcane Bolt", 75)).
  2. Print wizard.toString() (or just wizard).
  3. Print the signature spell's power.
  4. Create two identical Spell("Arcane Bolt", 75) instances and compare them with equals(). Print the result.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what Java records generate automatically, why they enforce immutability, and describe a case where using a record would be wrong — and what you'd use instead.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory: define a record Artifact(String name, int rarity) and a record Hero(String name, Artifact equipped). Create a Hero named "Kael" equipped with Artifact("Shadowblade", 5). Print the hero, print the artifact's rarity, and verify two identical Artifact instances are equal.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The implicitly generated record constructor that accepts all components and assigns them to the final fields.
A record constructor with no parameter list. The compiler appends field assignments automatically after the body, letting you focus on validation.
Two objects are equal if their components are equal, regardless of identity. Records implement this by default.
A class whose instances are considered equal purely by their state. Records are an explicit value-based construct in Java.
Record fields are implicitly final — they cannot be reassigned after construction, making records safe to share across threads.
Accessors for record components use the component name directly (e.g., name()) rather than the JavaBean convention (getName()).
Java records don't generate wither methods automatically, but you can write them manually: return new Spell(newName, this.power()).

questions.questionHtml: For record Wizard(String name, int level), what is the correct accessor call for the name?
questions.explanationHtml: Record accessors use the component name directly as a method — wizard.name(). Records do not follow the JavaBean getName() convention.
equals() on records compares components structurally, so a.equals(b) is true. But a == b checks reference identity — they are two distinct objects — so it is false.

questions.questionHtml: What is wrong with this record definition?
questions.correctAnswer: Records cannot declare instance fields beyond their components. The power field is already generated from the component list. Remove the extra field declaration.
questions.explanationHtml: Record bodies may only contain static fields, methods, constructors, and nested types. Instance fields are exclusively those declared in the component list. Declaring private int power inside the body is a compile error.

questions.questionHtml: In which scenario should you use a regular class instead of a record?
options: A DTO that carries name and age from an API response
A coordinate with x and y that needs structural equality
A shopping cart that adds, removes, and modifies items over time
A key in a HashMap that should compare by value
questions.correctAnswer: A shopping cart that adds, removes, and modifies items over time
questions.explanationHtml: Records are immutable — you cannot change their components after construction. A shopping cart requires mutable state (adding/removing items), so a regular class with mutable fields is the right tool. All other options describe immutable value objects that are ideal candidates for records.
